﴿كَأَنَّهُمْ أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍ﴾ "as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees." The meaning of their comparison to the trunks of palm trees was mentioned in al-Qamar. "Khawiyah" is that which has become empty through the long duration of its decay and corruption.

It is called al-Haqqah because it is certain to happen (tahuqq), that is, its existence is valid, and there is no doubt about its occurrence; or because it makes due to every person the recompense of his deeds; or because it reveals the realities of matters.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 69, verses 9–11:

﴿And those before him﴾ means those disbelieving nations who came before them. The closest of them to him were the people of Shu'ayb, and it is apparent that they are the ones intended, since ʿAd and Thamud have already been mentioned. The people of Lot are the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikat). The people of Noah have already been alluded to in His saying: ﴿When the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾. [The word] ﴿wa-man qablahu﴾ is read with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba' (qablahu, i.e., "and those before him"), and its meaning is: his troops and his followers. ﴿With the overturned﴾ (al-khati'ah) is either a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of the sin (al-khati'ah), or an adjective for an omitted noun whose estimated form is: "with the sinful deed." ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾: if the pronoun refers to Pharaoh and his people, then the messenger is Moses, peace be upon him; if it refers to the overturned cities, then the messenger is Lot, peace be upon him; and if it refers to all of them, then "the messenger" is a generic noun (ism jins) or means the message (al-risalah). ﴿Overwhelming (rabiyah)﴾ means great, and it derives from your saying: "rabā al-shay'" when a thing increased. ﴿The water overflowed﴾ is an expression for its abundance; it may be that it means it overflowed over the people of the earth, or over its treasurers, i.e., at the time of the flood of Noah, peace be upon him. ﴿We carried you in the sailing ship﴾: the sailing ship is the ark. If he means the ship of Noah, then the meaning of ﴿We carried you﴾ is "We carried your forefathers," because everyone on earth is from the offspring of Noah and his three sons who were with him in the ship. If he means the genus of ships, then the address is in its literal sense.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 69, verses 12–14:

﴿So that We might make it for you a reminder﴾ The pronoun refers to the act, which is the carrying in the ship. It was also said that it refers to the ship. If he means ships in general, then the meaning is that they are a reminder of the power and blessing of God for those who ride them or hear of them. If he means the ship of Noah, then it has been said that God preserved it until some of its planks were seen by the first of this Ummah. ﴿And a retaining ear may retain it﴾ The pronoun refers back to what the pronoun in "We might make it" refers to, and this strengthens that it refers to the act. The retaining ear (uthun wa'iyah) is the one that understands what it hears and preserves it. It is said: "I retained (waiytu) the knowledge" when one has acquired it. For this reason some have described it as the ear that has understood from God. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Ali ibn Abi Talib: "I have supplicated God that He make it your ear, O Ali." Ali said: "After that I did not forget anything I heard." Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'an ear, retaining' in the singular and indefinite, to indicate the scarcity of those who retain, to rebuke people for the small number among them who retain, and to indicate that a single ear, if it understands from God Most High, is the one regarded by God and not others." ﴿A single blast﴾ meaning the blast of the Trumpet, and it is the first. ﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ The pronoun refers to the earth and the mountains. The meaning of "dukkata" is that some of them are struck against others until they are crushed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Dakk (crushing) is more emphatic than daqq (pounding)." It was also said: its meaning is that they are spread out until the earth and the mountains become level.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 69, verses 18–24:

﴿On that Day you will be exposed; not a secret of yours will be hidden﴾. This is addressed to all of the world. "Exposure" (al-'ard) means the resurrection or the reckoning. ﴿Hidden﴾ means: no state hidden of your hopes (al-amal) and inner secrets. It may also mean that nothing of their bodies will be concealed, since they will be gathered barefoot and naked.

﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾. "Record" (al-kitab) here means the books of deeds (sahifat al-a'mal).

﴿Here, take and read my record!﴾ Ha'um (hā'um) is an ism al-fi'l (verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb meaning "take" or "come here"). Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "come here." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a sound from which the meaning "take" is understood. "Kitabiyah" (my record) is the object sought by ha'um, and "iqra'u" (read) is governed by the implied meaning. The sense is: "Ha'um, the record; iqra'u my record," and then the first object was omitted because the second indicates it, and the verb acted upon it. The second (iqra'u) is the view of the Basrans, while the first verb (ha'um) is the view of the Kufans. The evidence for the soundness of the Basran view is that if the first had governed it, one would say "iqra'uhu." The hā' in "kitabiyah" is for pause (al-waqf). Likewise in "hisabiyah," "maliyah," and "sultaniyah." The original form was that it should drop in connected speech, but it remains there in recitation out of regard for the script of the Mushaf. Hamza dropped it in connected speech.

The meaning of the verse: the servant who is given his record in his right hand says to the people, "Read my record," in a manner of joy and delight in his record.

﴿Indeed I was certain﴾. Here "zann" (supposition) means certainty (yaqin).

﴿In a pleasing life﴾. That is, one possessing pleasure (radiyah), like their saying "tamir" (possessing dates) for one who owns dates. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not the active participle form (ism fa'il). Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be an active participle, with the verb attributed to it metaphorically while it actually belongs to its possessor.

﴿Its clusters﴾. Plural of "qitf," which is what is picked from fruits, such as a bunch of grapes.

﴿Near at hand﴾. That is, close. It is related that the servant takes them with his mouth from their tree, in whatever state he is, whether standing, sitting, or reclining.

﴿Because of what you sent ahead in the days gone by﴾. That is, you advanced righteous deeds.

﴿In the days gone by﴾. That is, the past, meaning the days of the world.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 69, verse 30–37:

﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾. This is an address to the guards of Hell (al-zabaniyah), said to them either by God Most High or by the angels by God's command. ﴿Shackle him﴾ means: put a shackle (ghull) around his neck. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

﴿Its length is seventy cubits﴾. The meaning of "dhar‘uha" is its length. Scholars differed about this cubit (dhira‘). It was said: it is the well-known cubit. It was said: it is the cubit of the king. It was also said: the cubit is seventy spans (ba‘), each span being the distance between Makkah and Kufah. How well al-Hasan al-Basri put it in his saying: "God knows by which cubit it is." He made it seventy cubits to express its great length, for seventy is among the numbers by which the Arabs intend abundance. It is possible that this chain is for each one of the people of the Fire, or that it is shared among all of them. Al-Tha‘labi related this.

﴿Then thread him﴾, meaning: cause him to enter it. It is narrated that it coils around him until it encompasses him and squeezes him. According to this, the speech is in its proper sense, namely that he is threaded into it. The phrase "in a chain" is placed before "thread him" to express restriction (hasr), meaning: do not thread him except into this chain. Likewise, "the boiling water" is placed before "burn him" to express restriction as well.

﴿The food of the needy﴾. It may be that it means the feeding of a needy person, so the noun is placed in the position of a pronoun. Or it may be understood as: he did not urge the giving of food to the needy. He attributed the food to the needy because there is a relation between them. Describing him as one who did not urge the feeding of the needy indicates that he would not feed them himself, a fortiori. This verse shows the great merit and virtue of charity, for the withholding of food from the needy is linked with disbelief in God.

﴿So he has no friend here today﴾. On this there are two opinions: one is that he has no friend; the other is that he has no drink.

﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾. The hamim is hot water, and the ghislin, according to Ibn ‘Abbas, is the pus of the people of the Fire. It was also said: it is a tree which the people of the Fire eat. The lexicographers said: it is what flows from wounds when they are washed, and it is of the form fi‘lin, from the root "ghasl" (washing).

﴿Al-khati’un﴾ is the plural of khati’, who is one who does what is contrary to what is right deliberately, whereas the mukhti’ is one who does it without intention.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 69, verses 44–51:

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings,﴾ Taqawwul (fabricating speech) is to attribute to someone what he did not say. The meaning is: if We had punished him, none of you would have prevented him or defended him. The plural "hajizin" is used because "ahad" (one/anyone) carries the sense of a group. ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and it was also said it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is more apparent. ﴿And indeed, it is a cause of regret for the disbelievers.﴾ That is, a regret for them in the Hereafter, because they will feel remorse when they see the reward of the believers. ﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth (haqq al-yaqin).﴾ The Kufans said this is an idafa (construct) of a thing to itself, like your saying "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque). Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "the eye of certainty" (ʿayn al-yaqin) and "the pure essence of certainty" (mahd al-yaqin). Ibn 'Atiyya said: the skilled scholars went to the view that the truth (al-haqq) is attributed to the most eloquent of its aspects.
